name: veilid
desc: Peer-to-peer network for easily sharing various kinds of data
why: A peer-to-peer routing and DHT network with onion-style privacy; a real door into how decentralised networks actually work.

brief.what_it_is: Veilid is an open-source peer-to-peer framework, written in Rust with Flutter bindings, for building apps that exchange data without a central server. According to the homepage video, messages pass through other participating nodes, and those nodes cannot read the content because it is end-to-end encrypted. Every device running a Veilid app is a node, so the network is made of the apps themselves. The fetched pages do not describe inputs or outputs in technical detail. They describe a framework that developers build communication apps on, with VeilidChat as the first public beta app. The brew package installs two executables, veilid-cli and veilid-server.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a response to servers and intermediaries that can read, store, or sell private communications: "Privacy is a human right." The project's stated goal is to take the middle man out so that "it's just you and someone else chatting privately."
brief.how_it_works: According to the video transcript on the homepage, nodes relay messages between peers, and all content is encrypted end-to-end, so relaying nodes cannot read it. The video says the design is similar to Tor and IPFS but faster, and that the network is fully distributed with no servers storing data. I did not find a technical explanation of routing, DHT use, or onion-style layering in the pages I could read, so treat the mechanism as the project's own high-level description, not a verified account.
brief.install_notes: The brew package lists two executables, veilid-cli and veilid-server. I found no install or setup steps in the homepage, the GitLab page, or the README. The README contains only a line pointing to the wiki, and the wiki home page loaded empty. The homepage has a Developers section with a Download link, but I did not follow it, so I cannot confirm the download or build path. The video mentions Rust and Flutter bindings, which suggests a Rust toolchain for building from source, but that is inference, not documented.
brief.standout: The project sets out to be an application framework rather than a single chat app, and the homepage pitches the network as made up of every participating app acting as a relay node. The scout note's comparison to Tor and IPFS is the project's own marketing claim in the video, not something I verified.
brief.status: Active on the evidence I saw, but thin. The homepage announces a "New Public Beta Available for VeilidChat" dated 2026-09-28, and the page links to a changelog and a beta testing page. The GitLab repo was created July 4, 2023. I did not see a last-commit date or a release number, so I cannot confirm recent activity beyond the homepage announcement.
brief.caveats: The homepage is mostly marketing, and its claims (no servers, faster than Tor and IPFS, privacy for all) come from the project's own video and have not been checked. The README is a single line pointing to a wiki, and the wiki home loaded empty, so there is little technical documentation in the pages I could read. The license is Mozilla Public License 2.0, per GitLab. The video says it is written in Rust with Flutter bindings. I found no platform list and no build instructions. The homepage was reachable, but the "How it works" URL I guessed returned 404.

anyone can build any kind of communication app on top of it with privacy and security built in.

judge.reason: Veilid’s app-as-node privacy network is a worthwhile doorway into decentralized routing, though its thin documentation and marketing-heavy claims make the actual mechanics hard to assess.

entry.title: Veilid
entry.tldr: An open-source peer-to-peer app framework where every running app is a node that relays end-to-end encrypted data, with no central server in the middle.
entry.deeper_look:
Veilid is a framework for building apps that exchange data without a central server. According to the project's homepage video, every device running a Veilid app is a node. Messages pass through other participating nodes, and those nodes cannot read them because the content is end-to-end encrypted. The network is the apps themselves.

The project frames this as a response to servers and intermediaries that can read, store, or sell private communications. Its own line is "Privacy is a human right." The stated goal is to remove the middle man so that "it's just you and someone else chatting privately." It is written in Rust with Flutter bindings, and the first public app built on it is VeilidChat, currently in beta.

The idea underneath is the interesting part: a network with no operator, where relaying, storing and routing are all done by the participants. The video compares the design to Tor and IPFS and calls it faster. That is the project's own claim, and the pages read for this entry do not explain the routing mechanism in technical terms.

The brew package installs two executables, `veilid-server` and `veilid-cli`. The names suggest a node you run and a client to talk to it, but the documentation read for this entry does not confirm that. Expect to learn by reading source and `--help` output.

entry.whats_unique: It is pitched as a general application framework rather than a single chat app, with every participating app acting as a relay node.
entry.caveats: Documentation is thin: the README is one line pointing to a wiki that loaded empty, the homepage is mostly marketing, and its claims about speed and privacy are unverified.
